title: The Forger's Ledger
text:
The stairwell smelled like machine oil and cold concrete, the recycler drums somewhere below still running their angry twenty-fourth hour. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s terminal chirped again before he reached street level.

Not the client. A relay tag he half-recognized: FERENTI, C. - ARCHIVIST, DETROIT SPUR.

He'd taken the man's forty-one pages three weeks back, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a6c0-7bbd-b014-4496b7f489a7">Sable</entity>-routed, unremarkable - historical utility surveys, a security flat on top of the Read's rate. Paid, filed, done. Except <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> didn't ping closed contracts. Nobody did.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> opened it standing on the landing, one hand still on the rail.

FERENTI: THE PAGE CLEARED YOUR SCREEN. IT DID NOT CLEAR MINE. I AM ASKING YOU TO LOOK AGAIN BEFORE I FILE IT AS TRUTH.

He read it twice, same as the client's amendment, except this one didn't feel like weather. He thought about <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s tea cup turning its quarter-turn, the room he'd lost to his own archive, the man's voice going flat on *I become the reason the claim is clean.* <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had heard that shape of fear before - not the fear of getting hurt, the fear of being used as the good name on a bad thing. It was Vong's fear, some version of it, standing over a pot with his own franchise stamped on the side. It was, if he let himself sit in it for half a second on a stairwell that smelled like plastomer, his own.

He didn't sit in it. He typed back one line - *sending someone* - and thought about <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-602e-7a47-a1ec-61747fc9d537">Marisol</entity>.

She worked jobs like this cold, no names exchanged that mattered, and she never once needed the client to explain what "wrong" meant before she found it. Everyone <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew who'd used her once came back, and nobody had a bad word to say. If forty-one pages had a seam in them, she'd find which one, and she'd tell him after, exactly as promised, the way she told everyone after.

He pinged her handle. No preamble - she didn't like preamble.

KYLE: Archive job. <entity repo="place" guid="03964523-e47c-306f-ce05-cc8b80500139">Detroit</entity> spur. Forty-one pages, paper stock, already cleared once. Someone thinks a lie is sitting in a trusted stack. Need the page that doesn't belong.

The reply came back in under a minute, which for her was fast.

MARISOL: Anyone can take. The trick is putting something back. Send the address. I'll tell you after.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> sent it and kept moving, down through the recycler heat and out into the evening cold, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity>'s tremor climbing up through his boots from thirty meters under the street. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s forty-one pages were three weeks gone and none of his business anymore, except the man had asked him to look again, and <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had already decided to spend someone else's evening doing exactly that.

Behind him, the terminal chirped once more. He didn't look. Whatever the client wanted next, it could wait for the stairs to end.

She was already in the lobby, finishing a warm bun from the cart two doors down. Mid-forties, warm-faced, field coat the brown of autumn mud. She brushed the crumbs off her lapel and gave him a handshake that lasted the exact professional fraction of a second — the grip of someone who'd sized him up before he crossed the floor. She wasted no gesture. Her hands were steady and unremarkable until you noticed that.

"Marisol."

"<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>."

"I know." No agenda in it. "You held the carousel park last month. The whole block talked about it. The carousel ran music."

"Four bars."

"Four bars," she agreed, and they went upstairs.

He needed her signature on the records-access form before noon — one name in ink, and the sealed inventory would open to him for the rest of the case. That was all. Get the form in front of her, get it signed, get out before the screening flagged anything he'd rather keep unlisted. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> had rented this floor eleven years ago and spent every one of them turning it into the kind of place where paper lived longer than people did — sealed windows, the air dry enough to make <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s throat tight, the whole careful architecture of a life spent making sure nothing got lost.

The scanner on the third-floor landing gave its institutional chime — STANDARD SCREENING INITIATED — DOCUMENT INVENTORY — PSYKER ON PREMISES — VISITOR CONFIRM. Marisol confirmed without breaking stride, the way a woman does when she's been thumbing that same word since she was twenty-two. She didn't roll her eyes. Something in the set of her jaw took the word, weighed it, and decided not to spend the afternoon on it.

On the ride over he had thumbed <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> back to six. The trencher had cost him two, and he didn't walk into archives light.

The records room smelled of conservation solvent and old paper, which was better than the two floors below. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> ran the intake briskly and left them to it.

Marisol pulled on cotton archival gloves — soft, worn thin from use, worked on one finger at a time — and looked at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> over the first tray. "The way I work: I go through in order and tell you what I get. An authentic page has a whole person in it — the hands that made it, what they had for breakfast, whether they hated the job. A fake is just a job. Clean in a way nothing real is clean." She turned the first page. "I charge by the touch because it costs me by the touch."

Page one: clean.

Page fourteen: clean.

A knock at twenty-two — <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s runner, twelve or so, sleeve patches from a Spine courier house, the face of a kid who'd been doing piecework since he was ten. He held out more documents. "Broker says these came with the load. The <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="3b153287-1c59-41b7-8773-e63a11aea945">Psyk</entity> verify these too, or just the primaries?"

"Primaries," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, and tipped him Φ2, above rate.

When the door closed, Marisol said without looking up, "He'll grow out of the word or he won't. Not my afternoon."

Page twenty-three: clean. Eleven more after that. She moved through them methodically, one hand flat on each sheet, no half-second pause, no hitch that would mean the thing was telling her something.

At thirty-eight she stopped.

She held the page by its edges and laid her palm flat, fingers spread, and went still — the stillness of a woman listening to something that made no sound. Her breathing slowed. Her jaw tightened. "This one."

It was a utility survey of the carousel junction on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity>: the underground chamber, the trunk lines, the sub-floor hatch under the maintenance skirt. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew the room. He'd bled there. He knew the width of that hatch and the passage behind it and what the junction smelled like when the line was warm. He knew the half-block of stubborn green above it that had never made economic sense to any of the towers, and four bars of music that had played there before the mechanism wound down.

The survey read: SITE ASSESSED — NO ACTIVE INFRASTRUCTURE — DEAD GLASS — NO RELEVANT ASSETS.

He had stood in that room six weeks ago. The line had been humming.

"It's beautiful work," Marisol said. It was not a compliment. "The fiber, the aging chemistry, the hand — almost right. The paper's old, the ink's old. But the hands that made it didn't care about this survey. They cared about making a survey." She set it down like it was contaminated. "The gesture is wrong. The pressure is wrong. Whoever filled this out never filled out a survey before in their life." She lifted her palm off it. "There's your forgery. One specific lie: there's nothing at this address."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the date stamp. Three months old. Three months this page had sat in <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s archive, patient and filed, waiting for a demolition order that would find its provenance already clean. Dead glass on the record. Officially gone. No acquisition needed, no permit required — just a site that had never existed to argue with.

He held on to that.

Then the smell came in through the ventilation slit above the third tray: acetone, and something flatter under it — the chemistry of a fire agent primed and waiting.

Four seconds between the smell and the door.

The woman came first — chrome running her whole left arm, shoulder to fingertip, the hardware expensive enough not to show at the joint seams, a multi-tool already open on her palm with the incendiary trigger showing. Three men behind her. All four moved with the rehearsed economy of a team that had learned the room off a floor plan.

They did not say get away from the paper.

She said: "<entity repo="vocabulary" guid="816dbd83-fa5a-4ccb-9b58-b353707146d3">The Read</entity> comes with us. Principal wants her able to talk."

It landed on <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> all at once. The fire wasn't for the forgery. The fire was cover. The principal had decided that a woman who could touch a forged survey and feel the lie in its fiber was worth more than the paper. Paper you could burn. A witness you could carry, and the authentication walked out with the crew. No one else in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> was going to authenticate that forgery by hand.

"Marisol," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The window."

"I have eight pages and the forgery," she said, already moving, "and I am not leaving the forgery."

The tool discharged. Blue-white in the back corner, the third tray catching. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> put <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity>'s first round through the multi-tool at the wrist joint — the percussion enormous in the narrow room — and the augmentation's servos screamed, a high mechanical shriek under the roar of the fire, and the woman sat down hard around the nerve hit, the tool spinning off into the flames. One spent. Five left. The room was burning now.

Two of the men moved to bracket Marisol, not <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. A mistake. <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> came out and wrote a clean line across the nearer one's wrist flexors — wide of anything that wouldn't grow back — and he found a new priority and took it to the floor. The second got a hand on Marisol's field coat and got <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s elbow across the hinge of his jaw. The cheap fast answer, when the clean one would cost tenths of a second the room didn't have.

The fourth — hired for position, slowest to commit — watched three colleagues turn into problems and put his effort into the door.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> let him go. There was no version of this where chasing him put the fire out.

His left shoulder had taken the woman's elbow on the way down, outside the mesh. It hurt in a clean, specific way: bruised, not broken, still working. He set the pain aside and kept moving.

"Extinguisher," Marisol said. "Beside the door."

She had the forgery and a stack of pages under her arm and was working through the surviving trays with the calm of a woman who charged by the touch — fingertips skating each sheet, reading the weave for heat damage the way she read it for forgery, salvaging by feel what the <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aa93-73ed-b61d-b7955f44a2d8">cold storage</entity> had kept at fifty-two degrees and thirty-five percent for a century because that was the temperature old paper liked to stay honest at.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> found the extinguisher and killed the blaze — blue, then grey, then out.

One round spent. Five left. The shoulder would keep. Third tray gone.

The fourth man had a van, and the van had a frequency <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> could track. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had pulled the plate off the lobby scanner — <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> registration, recent, a gray panel job with no markings, the kind of vehicle built to dissolve into traffic because it looked like every other panel-side van in the city. Marisol had the forgery. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> had his surviving thirty-eight pages and his grief for the Domazinski surveys, gone to ash in the third tray. Somewhere below them the extruder drums were still running the twenty-third hour without a pause.

Marisol set the forgery face-up on <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s table and laid a hand flat beside it, gloves singed at the cuff from the tray she'd handled like something that had just tried to kill her. "You should know what you were holding," she told him. "Worth a woman with a chrome arm and three men walking armed into a registered archive. Not for the paper — they'd have let the paper burn. For the pair of hands that could tell you it was a lie."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> wrote something in his log. His pen was not quite steady. He didn't look up from the ledger, cataloguing his losses like the number would hold still if he counted it right.

Outside the window the van's frequency had gone quiet. It had turned south on <entity repo="place" guid="01a06ee1-849c-7793-bce8-ae238e4576f6">Leavitt</entity> and not hurried. The fourth man hadn't gone to a hospital — no reason to, he'd walked out clean. He'd gone to file a report. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> knew how those moved: a name, a plate, a location routed up through whoever held the contract, timestamped so nobody upstream could pretend they'd been slow. He gave it six minutes before that report reached someone with the staff to send a second team.

"<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> asked. "Is there a back way?"

There was.

The back way was a stairwell that smelled of standing water and the mineral rot of old rebar — a service core built for a building that had been sold four times since anyone drew the plans. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went first. Marisol came behind him with the forgery pressed flat against her chest under the field coat, both arms wrapped around it like the one thing she wasn't going to let the floor have if she fell.

"Two flights down, then the loading apron," <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> had said. "Nobody uses it. Half the lights are dead."

Half was optimistic. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted three working fixtures in five flights, and the dark between them had a texture to it — humid, close, threaded with a smell like a basement that had flooded once and never fully forgiven the building for it. The rails hummed at a frequency his neuretics picked up and filed — the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> corridor running somewhere underneath, close enough to put a tremor in the steel.

He heard them before he saw them. Boots on metal, unhurried, from below.

Not the four from upstairs. A different cadence — heavier, paced, the sound of people who'd been told to wait at the bottom of this specific stairwell and had nowhere else to be. A team that had walked the building in their heads before they walked it with their bodies. <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity>'s back way had a name because someone besides <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> knew about it.

"Up," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said.

"Up is the fire," Marisol said.

"Up is a fire that's already out. Down is new."

She didn't argue. She turned, and that was when the landing above them opened and a third element came through it — not the chrome-arm woman, not her three. A fifth man, fresh, blocking the return route, already moving on the read that they'd hit the middle of the stairwell and had nowhere to go but sideways.

There was no sideways. Six feet of stair, a rail gone soft with rust, a drop through the gap that would break something on the way down if anyone went through it.

The man above didn't have a name <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> needed. He had a collapsible baton, extended with a flick, the kind with weight enough to break bone, and the specific confidence of someone who thought two flights of blind stairwell was a controlled space.

It wasn't. It was <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s kind of space — too narrow for numbers to matter, too dark for optics, close enough that <entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> was a liability and <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> was the only tool that made sense.

He put himself between Marisol and the baton and let the man commit to the first swing.

The stairwell took the shock of it — steel ringing off steel where the baton clipped the rail on the man's own backswing, an amateur's tell, the kind of mistake nobody made twice. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't need him to make it twice. He came in under the arc, put his shoulder into the man's sternum, and drove him back into the wall hard enough that the whole flight shuddered underfoot and the man lost the air in his lungs.

Below, the boots picked up their pace. The sound of a decision made — the moment they stopped climbing and started positioning.

Marisol's voice, flat, working the math out loud the way she worked a page: "How many is down there."

"Don't know."

"How many can you take."

"Don't know that either." He got a hand on the baton man's wrist, turned it until the tool clattered free and rang off three steps before it stopped. "Get behind me and stay on the page."

"I'm not leaving the—"

"I know."

The stairwell lights buzzed, one of the three working fixtures giving up mid-flicker, and for two full seconds they had almost no light at all — just the shapes of boots coming up through the dark and the man against the wall finding his feet again and the forgery a flat pressure against Marisol's ribs, the only clean thing in the whole shaft.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s shoulder throbbed where the elbow had caught it upstairs — a distinct, separate ache from whatever was about to happen to the rest of him. He filed it. There'd be time to itemize later, if later showed up.

"New plan," he said, and it came out level, the read-out voice, the one he used on kids and on rooms about to go very wrong at once. "We go through them. Not around. Through."

Marisol looked at the drop through the rail, then at the boots closing the last flight, then at him.

"Through costs what," she said.

He didn't answer that. There wasn't a clean number for it yet, and she'd know a lie the same way she knew a forged survey — by the fiber, by what a truth cost him to say.

The first of them came around the landing below, and the light went out for good.

The dark didn't stay total. A hand-lamp clicked on below — not aimed at them, aimed at the wall, throwing enough backscatter to work by without blinding the crew that carried it. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> counted the shapes it caught: three, maybe four, moving in a formation too clean for scavengers.

The one in front wasn't carrying a baton.

She came around the landing already turning, weight low, one arm out in a guard that wasn't defending her face — it was clearing a lane. Small unit on her forearm, matte, no manufacturer stamp <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> recognized, but the shape told him enough. Contact tool. Wrist-mounted. Bare polymer framework with capacitor nodes riding the joints — the kind built to reach past a guard and stop a nervous system from talking to itself. Five, ten seconds of nothing. Long enough to restrain. Long enough to extract.

She wasn't looking at <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>.

She tracked past him like he was furniture and put her eyes on Marisol — on the arms wrapped around the forgery, on the field coat, on the one target in the stairwell that mattered to whoever was paying for this. The three behind her fanned to hold <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> off the intercept, not to fight him. To buy her the two seconds she needed.

*Specialist.* The word arrived flat and unbidden, the read-out voice talking to himself now instead of a scared kid. *Somebody sent a specialist for the woman, not the man with the sword.*

He didn't have time to sit with what that meant — that the whole stairwell, the baton, the four upstairs, all of it might have been noise around this one narrow purpose. He had time to move.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> stepped into the lane instead of holding his ground behind Marisol. Wrong tactic on paper — should've kept the choke point, made them come through him one at a time. He did it anyway, because the woman's arm was already extending, because two more feet of stairwell was all the room the contact unit needed, and there wasn't a version of this where he watched it land from a safe distance.

She adjusted. Fast — faster than the baton man, faster than anyone upstairs. Weight shifted off the read of where he'd been rather than where he was, the tool tracking his shoulder instead of Marisol's collarbone by maybe four inches.

Four inches wasn't a miss. It was a mistake he could still make.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> got his forearm up. Not clean — the wrists complained, the left one pulling taut and hot as the muscle underneath fought the angle — and the guard he threw wasn't the two-handed turn <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity> wanted, wasn't the shape eleven years of discipline had built into his hands. It was whatever the half-second gave him. He caught her forearm on the outside instead of the inside, took the contact point off-line by inches, and ate the discharge through the meat of his shoulder instead of center mass.

It went through him like a struck bell — like someone had poured current into the muscle and found the ground it was looking for. Every nerve from collarbone to fingertip rang once, hard, and went dead.

He didn't go down. He wanted to note that for later, filed next to the shoulder and the wrist and the rib that had already spent its complaints for the week. His arm hung. It hadn't asked permission to stop working; it had simply stopped, the hand at the end of it curled loose and useless around nothing, the fingers opening because they had no say in it anymore.

The specialist recalibrated in the time it took him to notice his own arm was gone. She didn't waste the opening and she didn't hurry it — resetting the way someone resets when they've been paid to be thorough, already reading the fact that he'd lost half his mobility, already writing off the miss and pricing the next strike. She hadn't hit her target. She was resetting for the one <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafa-70f3-b5f5-be3330461876">still standing</entity> behind him.

"Down," Marisol said — not a question this time, an instruction, and she was already moving under his dead arm toward the gap in the rail rather than away from it, because up was the four and down was the crew and the only door nobody had covered yet was six feet of empty air and a floor that would break something on the way through.

They came out into the freight alley. Recycler heat vented up through a floor grate, and a lumen mouse ran the gutter seam, its thread bright in the grey. Marisol still had the forgery in her coat and the archival gloves on her hands.

She sat on a crate. "I want to do the delivery. If you have the object."

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-5f86-7b4e-ba08-349d6ddac1c7">Ferenti</entity> produced a courier glove from his coat pocket — he'd pulled it during the exit. One archival sleeve, right hand. He'd had the sense.

Marisol held it without ceremony. Soft leather, reinforced at the palm, the kind of thing a professional runner wore to keep their prints off a delivery. Standard. Forgettable. The kind of thing that got handed off a thousand times a day in <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> and never thought about again. She went quiet for almost a full minute, the extruder heat <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aaa1-7cec-8b36-549dcfb312fe">drifting</entity> over them.

"This glove's been on a lot of hands," she said. "Couriers pass gear around." Her thumb moved along the heel of the palm. "But the last hands that used it with purpose — they're in here. And the client feels like nobody." She held it up without looking at it. "No history. No preference. No person in the material at all. I've read forgers, collectors, thieves. Everyone leaves something. This is clean the way a room is clean after it's been prepared." She set it down. "The client feels like a job with no client in it."

Then her hand stopped moving.

She picked the glove up again, slower this time, the way you go back to a word you thought you'd read right. The contact came through her fingertips like a voice speaking in a language she'd learned before she had words for it — not the accumulated residue of a courier's hands, sweat and salt and the minor friction of a thousand deliveries, but something turned up, made sharper, made *clearer*.
